walkthroughs.body_html:
Enzymes — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Enzymes brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Enzymes.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: An enzyme stops working above its optimum temperature because:
options: it dissolves
its active site changes shape (denatures)
substrate runs out
it loses water

mcqs.q: Which is the best optimum pH for pepsin (in stomach)?
options: pH 2
pH 7
pH 9
pH 13

mcqs.q: What happens to an enzyme when it is denatured?
options: The enzyme has died because enzymes are alive.
Its tertiary structure (3D shape) changes, particularly the active site, so it can no longer bind substrate effectively.
The enzyme has been completely broken into amino acids.
Antibodies are tiny knives that physically cut pathogens apart.

mcqs.q: Why are enzymes specific to certain substrates?
options: Each enzyme can react with any substrate, but works fastest with one type.
Enzymes choose their substrate based on which one is most common in the cell.
Only substrates with complementary shape and chemistry to the active site can bind effectively.
Antibodies are tiny knives that physically cut pathogens apart.

mcqs.q: What makes antibodies effective against pathogens?
options: They have a specific shape complementary to antigens on a particular pathogen, marking it for destruction or neutralising it.
Antibodies are general-purpose proteins that work against any pathogen.
Enzymes choose their substrate based on which one is most common in the cell.
Antibodies are tiny knives that physically cut pathogens apart.
